"Documents" are not classified arbitrarily; they are classified because of content. An email is not in and of itself "Personally Identifiable Information" (as defined by NIST guidelines), but an email that contains PII is subject to all laws and regulations for the handling of PII.

The same goes for classified documents - a document containing classified information will at minimum meet the classification of the highest-level information contained within; sometimes the whole document might be classified at a higher level (Controlled->Confidential->Secret->Top Secret [Need-to-Know]) due to the fact that compiled information might be more sensitive than its parts.

It's for this reason that even when classified documents are "declassified," some portions of it may still be unavailable; some secrets are declassified after a decade, some after a century.

Ergo, an email with classified information in it is implicitly classified.

This information was not "classified retroactively," it was classified when accessed, classified when stored, and classified when deleted. The last of these three brings in another, unrelated problem in that Hillary Clinton acted in contempt of court in regards to violating orders to not delete said information pending federal investigation - despite claims that what was deleted was "private and not pertinent to State Department affairs," such claims are of no consequence and do not justify violation of court order.

So, even if you completely disregard the Clintons' violation of the Espionage Act with flimsy arguments that "it wasn't classified!" you're still left with two felonies:

  1. Federal Records Act - the use of non-government networks to transmit and store federal information, unclassified or not, is a federal offense due to major, major security vulnerabilities that are opened. Furthermore, the FRA requires preservation of all information transmitted as part of government affairs; the deletion of the email archive on the server violates this statute.
  2. Contempt of court - see above.
